title: Value types vs reference types (copy vs alias)
hook: When you assign a variable in C#, you either copy the data itself or copy a pointer to an object. That copy-versus-alias rule is the heart of value types and reference types.

blocks.text: C# splits types into two families. **Value types** (`struct`, `enum`, and built-in numerics like `int`, `bool`, `decimal`) store their data directly in the variable. Assigning `b = a` copies every field. **Reference types** (`class`, arrays, `string`, delegates) store a reference (think: a pointer) to an object on the heap. Assigning `list2 = list1` makes two variables point at the same object — changes through one are visible through the other.

entries.plainDefinition: A type whose assignment copies the actual data. Built-in numerics, `bool`, `decimal`, `struct`, and `enum` are value types.
entries.example: `var b = a;` where `a` is a `DateTimeOffset` — `b` gets its own copy.

entries.plainDefinition: A type whose assignment copies a reference to a shared object, not the object's contents.
entries.example: `var list2 = list1;` — both variables see the same `List<int>`.

entries.plainDefinition: Wrapping a value type inside an `object` (or interface) reference on the heap. It allocates memory and copies the value.
entries.example: `object boxed = 199;` boxes the `int` 199 into a heap object.

blocks.text: Confusing copy and alias causes subtle bugs. You mutate a struct from a list indexer and wonder why the list did not change — you mutated a **copy**, not the element in the list. You pass a `List<T>` to two methods and one clears it — the other sees an empty list because they share the same object. **Boxing** in hot loops (storing `int` in non-generic collections) creates garbage the Garbage Collector (GC) must clean up — details in module 14.

blocks.title: Interview framing
blocks.body: Say: "value assignment copies data; reference assignment aliases an object." Do not claim "structs always live on the stack" — the CLR may store a value in a register, on the stack, or boxed on the heap. Stack versus heap is an implementation detail covered in the memory module.

sections.heading: How it works step by step

items.title: Value type assignment
items.body: The runtime copies all fields byte-for-byte. `a` and `b` are independent — changing `b` does not affect `a`.

items.title: Reference type assignment
items.body: Only the reference (address) is copied. Both variables point to one object. `list2.Add(1)` changes what `list1` sees.

items.title: Boxing a value
items.body: Assigning a value type to `object` or a non-generic interface wraps it in a heap object. This is an allocation you pay for.

items.title: Unboxing
items.body: Casting the boxed object back to the original value type copies the value out. A wrong cast throws `InvalidCastException`.

snippet.label: Independent structs vs aliased lists
snippet.explanation: Lines 1–2: `DateTimeOffset` is a struct (value type). `b = a` copies all fields. Lines 4–7: `List<int>` is a class (reference type). `list2 = list1` aliases the same list; adding through `list2` is visible on `list1`.

snippet.label: Boxing and unboxing
snippet.explanation: Line 2: assigning `int` to `object` boxes the value on the heap. Line 4: unboxing with `(int)` extracts the `int`. Line 7: unboxing to the wrong type throws — you must match the original boxed type.

snippet.label: Struct copy trap in a list
snippet.explanation: Line 3: the indexer returns a **copy** of the struct, not a reference to the slot. Line 4: changing `p.X` does not update the list. Line 7: assign back with `with` (or write `points[0] = p` after mutation) to replace the element.

blocks.title: Copy vs alias
rows: Primitives: by value; objects: by reference

blocks.title: Pitfalls to avoid
blocks.body: Mutating a struct from a list indexer and expecting the list to change — you mutated a copy. Boxing value types in hot loops (non-generic collections, `object` keys) then blaming GC without measuring. Thinking `string` is a value type because `==` compares content — it is a reference type with value-like equality.

blocks.text: How to prove it in production: `nint` and `nuint` (C# 9+) are native-sized integer value types — they copy like any other struct and are useful for pointer-sized indices and interop without casting to `IntPtr`. On 64-bit runtimes, `nint` is 8 bytes; assignment copies the value, not a heap object. Measure boxing with dotnet-counters (`GC Allocation Rate`) when legacy APIs take `object`. In module 14 you will map stack versus heap; here the language rule is copy versus alias, not storage location.

snippet.label: nint as a value type for native-sized indices
snippet.explanation: Line 1: `nint` is a struct (value type). Line 2–4: assignment copies; incrementing `copy` does not change `rowCount`. Lines 7–8: `nint` bridges to `IntPtr` without treating the index as a reference type.

blocks.title: Tradeoffs at senior level
rows: Not a reference — do not confuse with IntPtr boxing
Prefer generics to avoid GC pressure

blocks.title: What gets you rejected in interviews
blocks.body: Saying all structs live on the stack. Claiming `string` is a value type because == compares content. Not knowing that `nint` is a value type. Explaining boxing without mentioning that it allocates on the heap.

interviewTakeaways: Value assignment copies data; reference assignment aliases an object.
Boxing wraps a value type on the heap — measure with GC counters in hot paths.
`nint`/`nuint` are native-sized value types; they copy like int, not like a class.
60s: Copy vs alias is the rule. nint is a struct. string is a reference type with value equality. Boxing allocates. Stack/heap is module 14.
Follow-up: why does mutating a struct from list[i] not update the list?
commonPitfalls: Saying structs always live on the stack gets you rejected — location is a CLR detail.
Thinking nint is a reference type because it relates to pointers.
Strong answer: 'Assignment copies values or aliases references. nint copies like int. Boxing allocates. Stack versus heap is implementation.'

jsTsCorrelations.note: JavaScript primitives copy on assignment; objects alias. C# makes the same split explicit with value types (`struct`) and reference types (`class`).
